newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's capital markets fall short of most.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's capital markets fall short of most.

text.p: After starting the 1990s as a favorite of international investors, Argentina's capital markets have failed to develop and are still among the smallest of the emerging markets.

Of the 26 emerging markets classified by the World Bank's International Finance Corporation, Argentina is grouped with Hungary, Poland and Venezuela at the bottom of the ranking in terms of the number of companies listed on each country's stock exchange.
In fact the number of listings on the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange is actually shrinking.

The bourse quoted 240 companies in 1983, but this had fallen to 179 by 1990 and to 149 today. Turnover is down too on the bourse's heyday in 1992, when it handled $65 million a day. Nowadays volume averages around $15 million.

Investors were onced lured in droves to Argentina after President Carlos Menem took office in 1989 and launched sweeping economic reforms. Privatizations including the $6 billion sale of oil firm YPF and a $5 billion telecommunications sell-off greatly increased local market capitalization.

But today, the exchange's market capitalization equals about 14 percent of Argentina's gross domestic product (GDP), half the relative size of the Brazilian and Mexican markets. The capitalization of the Santiago Stock Exchange is three times greater in terms of its proportion of Chilean GDP, according to private consultancy Estudio Rossi.

"This means that Argentine companies, in their growth strategies, are finding it more efficient to complement the reinvestment of profits with taking on debt rather than looking for new shareholders," said Ricardo Schefer, an economist for the Proeco consultancy.
While it is common for Argentine companies to issue bonds abroad, it is rare for them to sell shares. Capital increases on the stock market are even less usual.

Analysts said that one of the reasons for the stock market's unpopularity is that companies have to pay tax on profits generated from their own capital. But if they finance investment with debt, 30 percent of their interest payments are tax-deductable.
But Macchi said that the Buenos Aires market meets international standards in efficient provision of information, transparency of operations and in the guarantees of payment.
He admitted however that operating on the market is still too expensive.
Macchi said that there is a great demand from companies to float on the exchange.
"But the Tequila Effect and the political uncertainty that surrounded the former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo put slowed everything down," he said.
The so-called "Tequila Effect" of Mexico's shock devaluation in December 1994 caused investors to stampede out of emerging markets and tipped Argentina into recession.
